candidate.blueprint_locator: Physiological Integrity → Basic Care and Comfort, printed p. 11 (PDF p. 15): related activity statement 'Evaluate the client’s nutritional status and intervene as needed,' within care and comfort activities.
candidate.blueprint_topic: Nutritional-status assessment and individualized dietary support
candidate.educational_objective: Recognize when sodium restriction is contributing to poor intake and sarcopenia in cirrhosis and collaborate to individualize the diet so ascites management does not prevent adequate nutrition.

options.A: Assess the client's nutritional status and collaborate with the dietitian and treating team to individualize the diet; sodium restriction may need adjustment if it is preventing adequate intake.
options.B: Intensify sodium restriction regardless of intake because preventing ascites is more important than maintaining adequate nutrition.
options.C: Tell the client to stop eating protein and calories until the ascites improves so fluid retention will decrease more quickly.
options.D: Ignore the weight and muscle loss because malnutrition is expected in cirrhosis and does not change the nutrition plan.

candidate.rationale: A is correct. AASLD guidance recognizes malnutrition and sarcopenia as important complications of cirrhosis and notes that sodium restriction can make food less palatable and reduce oral intake. When a sodium-restricted diet is preventing a client from meeting nutritional targets, the diet should be individualized and liberalization of sodium restriction can be considered in collaboration with the treating team and nutrition professionals. B is incorrect because a rigid restriction that worsens malnutrition may cause more harm and should be reassessed. C is incorrect because calorie and protein deprivation promotes catabolism and muscle loss rather than treating ascites. D is incorrect because malnutrition and sarcopenia are clinically important and require active assessment and intervention. The final item is distinct from V2-Q1842: it tests recognition of nutrition compromise from an overly restrictive diet rather than the misconception that protein should be restricted in hepatic encephalopathy.
candidate.source_claim_supported: Current AASLD guidance directly supports active assessment of malnutrition in cirrhosis and individualized sodium restriction when poor palatability or restrictive diets prevent adequate oral intake.
candidate.source_document_title: Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis; Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis
candidate.source_locator: AASLD 'Back to Basics: Outpatient Management of Cirrhosis' → 'Malnutrition in Cirrhosis': sodium restriction can decrease food palatability and create a barrier to adequate oral intake; liberalization should be considered in patients who are malnourished on a sodium-restricted diet. AASLD 'Malnutrition in the Adult with Cirrhosis' → nutrition interventions: restrictive diets may worsen intake; liberalization of sodium restriction should be considered when nutritional targets cannot be maintained.

candidate.stem: A client with cirrhotic ascites is following a sodium-restricted diet but is now eating very little and losing muscle mass because the food is unpalatable. Which nursing action is most appropriate?
